results.claim: Under the recorded definition, an AVL search tree is a Weak Search Tree supporting every insertion and deletion, including rebalancing, in deterministic O(log(n+2)) worst-case time.
results.proof_sketch: Initialize an empty AVL tree. Each node stores a distinct key, two child pointers, and a constant-size balance factor. Maintain (i) the BST invariant and (ii) subtree-height difference at most one. For any node and keys l,r in its left and right subtrees, respectively, the BST invariant gives l<key(node)<r, hence l<r; therefore every maintained tree satisfies the WST invariant. Insert by BST descent and leaf attachment. Delete a node with two children by replacing its key with its inorder successor and deleting that successor; otherwise splice out the node directly. Repair balance bottom-up. At a left-heavy node z, let y be its left child and let A,B,C be y's left subtree, y's right subtree, and z's right subtree. If h(A)>=h(B), right-rotate z; otherwise left-rotate y and then right-rotate z. With a=h(A), b=h(B), c=h(C), imbalance gives 1+max(a,b)=c+2. In the first case a=c+1 and b is c or c+1, which directly verifies both post-rotation balance inequalities. In the second case a=c and b=c+1; the two children of B have heights at most c and differing by at most one, so the double rotation leaves both children of the new root at height c+1. Right-heavy cases are symmetric. Rotations preserve inorder order, hence the BST invariant. There is constant work per ancestor. Finally, the minimum number M(h) of nodes in an AVL tree of height h satisfies M(h)=1+M(h-1)+M(h-2), so M(h)>=2^floor(h/2) and h=O(log(n+2)).

final_writeup:
Construction and proof.

Maintain an ordinary AVL tree, initialized empty. A node contains one distinct key, left and right child pointers, and a balance factor in {-1,0,1}; the balance factor is used only for rebalancing, never as a search router. Maintain the stronger invariant

all keys in left(v) < key(v) < all keys in right(v)

and the AVL height invariant |h(left(v))-h(right(v))|<=1. The stronger ordering immediately implies the WST condition: if a is anywhere in the left subtree and b anywhere in the right subtree, then a<key(v)<b, hence a<b. Thus every state of this data structure is a WST according to Definition 1.

Insertion follows ordinary key comparisons to a null child and attaches a new leaf. Deletion searches for the key. A node with at most one child is spliced out. For a node with two children, replace its key by the least key in its right subtree and splice out that successor. These operations preserve strict BST order before balancing and modify heights only on one root-to-leaf ancestor chain.

Walk back along that chain, updating balance factors. If a node has balance +2, perform a single right rotation when its left child is left-heavy or balanced, and a left-right double rotation otherwise. Use the mirror operations for balance -2. The height calculation in the claim proves that each case restores balance. A rotation preserves the inorder sequence of the involved subtrees and keys, so it preserves the strict BST invariant and consequently the WST invariant. After deletion, rebalancing may continue through every ancestor, but each ancestor needs at most two rotations and constant additional work. Insertion has the same O(h) upper bound.

For completeness, with null height -1, the minimum AVL size satisfies M(-1)=0, M(0)=1, and M(h)=1+M(h-1)+M(h-2). Induction gives M(h)>=2^floor(h/2), so an n-node AVL tree has height at most 2 log2(n)+O(1). Searching, the structural update, and all rebalancing therefore take deterministic O(log(n+2)) worst-case time per operation.

This resolves the recorded target literally: the source definition expressly permits BSTs as WSTs, and the target does not require maintaining genuinely non-BST key placements or accepting an arbitrary pre-existing WST. A strengthened question imposing either requirement would not be resolved by this construction, but that restriction is absent from the recorded statement.
checks_performed: Read only the designated JSON input; used no web source and inspected no other repository file.
Checked the AVL rotation height algebra for both single- and double-rotation cases; right-heavy cases follow by symmetry.

Ran an inline exact-integer enumeration of every admissible left-heavy height configuration through height 13, including child-height refinements for double rotations; every repaired configuration satisfied the AVL inequalities.
Computed the minimum-node recurrence through height 64 and checked M(h)>=2^floor(h/2) exactly.

As a scope sanity check, exhaustively enumerated WST labelings of several right-rotation shapes up to 11 nodes and confirmed that rotations on arbitrary non-BST WSTs need not preserve the weak invariant; this is why the construction deliberately maintains the stronger invariant.
